newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair sets out goals for government.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair sets out goals for government.

text.p: Labour leader Tony Blair on Tuesday laid out a "performance contract" with Britain and set his main goal as improving education after an election that opinion polls make him odds-on favourite to win.
In a rallying call to his last party conference before the election, due in the next seven months, Blair pledged to build Britain into the "skill superpower of the world".

In a stirring appeal to people from across the political spectrum to back him and end 17 years of Conservative rule, Blair pledged to rule for everybody and not just narrow interests on the Left or for the unions.
"I say to the British people, have the courage to change now, we are coming home to you," Blair said to loud applause in his keynote speech to the conference.
"No more squandering the nation's assets, no more sleaze... no more lies, no more broken promises. I say to the Tories (Conservatives) enough is enough. Enough, be done, be gone."
In his 10-point "performance contract for government" Blair vowed to
- boost the proportion of national income spent on education
- cut spending on "the welfare bills of social failure"
- cut spending on health bureaucracy and improve patient care
- cut the number of long-term unemployed
- halve the time it takes to get young offenders to court
- keep government borrowing and inflation low
- keep tax promises
- cut school class sizes
- devolve power to Scotland and Wales
- build a new and constructive relationship in Europe.
Blair promised to reverse Conservative policy by signing the European social chapter, which standardises conditions for workers across the European Union, before the end of 1997.
But he said he would not get rid of Britain's opt-out on a single currency, deciding to join only if it was in Britain's interests and only with the consent of the British people.
He warned there would be no return to the tax-and-spend policies of Labour governments in the past, vowing instead to govern as "the party of sound finance and good housekeeping".

Labour, out of power since 1979, heads the ruling Conservatives in polls by more than 20 points. Blair aims to cement that lead by convincing voters that he, more than Prime Minister John Major, is in touch with their aspirations.

Major, whose party has won four consecutive terms of office but is now dogged by voters' belief it is completely out of touch, was delivered a new blow on Tuesday when a Conservative MP dropped a legal fight against newspaper sleaze charges.

Neil Hamilton, who quit as a junior trade minister in 1994 after the Guardian allegations he had accepted cash in return for asking questions in parliament, maintains his innocence but said he could no longer afford to continue his libel fight.

But his decision was described by the Guardian's editor Alan Rusbridger as "one of the most astonishing cave-ins in the history of the law of libel" and the newspaper immediately repeated its allegations with additional details.
The row is likely to rumble on through next week's Conservative conference which Major is banking on to lift his flagging support and rally anxious party workers.
Blair lost no time in rubbing salt in the wound, warning Major that in government Labour would crack down on sleaze.
